questions.context: A student is telling her friend what she did last night before an important exam.
questions.instruction: Find and correct the single grammar error in this sentence: 'I knew I must study harder, but I spent the whole evening watching videos instead.'
questions.hint: Think about which modal verb fits a personal feeling of obligation in the past — 'must' doesn't work in past tense here.
questions.correctAnswer: I knew I should study harder, but I spent the whole evening watching videos instead.
questions.explanation: 'Must' has no past tense form for obligation, so we use 'should' to express that feeling of 'it would be the right thing to do' in the past.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: I knew I must studied harder, but I spent the whole evening watching videos instead.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Adding '-ed' to 'studied' after 'must' looks like a past fix, but you can't change the main verb like that — the whole modal needs to change to 'should'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: I knew I had to study harder, but I spent the whole evening watching videos instead.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Had to' is a valid past obligation form, but the sentence already uses 'knew', and 'should' fits the regret/advice meaning here more naturally than 'had to'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: I knew I must have studied harder, but I spent the whole evening watching videos instead.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Must have studied' is a past deduction ('I guess you studied'), not a simple obligation — it changes the meaning of what the student is trying to say.

questions.context: A student is describing his usual routine to a new classmate.
questions.instruction: Find and correct the single grammar error in this sentence: 'After lectures, I usually go to a library on campus to review my notes.'
questions.hint: Think about whether the library being mentioned is a specific, known place — and if so, which article fits.
questions.correctAnswer: After lectures, I usually go to the library on campus to review my notes.
questions.explanation: Because 'on campus' tells us exactly which library is meant, it's a specific place both speakers understand, so 'the' is the right article, not 'a'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: After lectures, I usually go to library on campus to review my notes.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Dropping the article entirely isn't right here — 'library' is a singular countable noun referring to a specific place, so it needs 'the'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: After the lectures, I usually go to a library on campus to review my notes.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: You've added 'the' to 'lectures' but left 'a library' unchanged — the error was with 'library', which refers to a specific known place and needs 'the'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: After lectures, I usually go to the library on the campus to review my notes.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Changing 'on campus' to 'on the campus' introduces a new error — 'on campus' is a fixed phrase that doesn't take an article, and the fix only needed 'a' → 'the' before 'library'.

questions.context: Two classmates are chatting before a group study session. One says: 'When we arrived at the café, the others ________ (already / order) their drinks and found a big table for all of us.'
questions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb. Use the words in brackets as a guide.
questions.hint: One action was fully finished before the other past action happened — which tense shows that earlier completion?
questions.explanation: The ordering happened before the arrival, so the past perfect 'had already ordered' is needed to show that earlier completed action.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: Leaving out 'had' gives you simple past, which doesn't show that the ordering was finished before the others arrived — the past perfect needs both words.
Past continuous describes an action in progress at that moment, but the sentence says they found a table too, suggesting everything was done before the group arrived.
Present perfect talks about a connection to now, but the whole sentence is set in the past — 'had already ordered' keeps everything in the past timeline.

questions.context: A tutor is giving written feedback to a student who struggles to stay focused.
questions.instruction: Find and correct the single grammar error in this sentence: 'The tutor suggested to take short breaks every 45 minutes to improve concentration.'
questions.hint: Think about which verb form follows 'suggest' — does it take a to-infinitive or an -ing form?
questions.correctAnswer: The tutor suggested taking short breaks every 45 minutes to improve concentration.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form), never a to-infinitive, so 'taking' is the correct choice after 'suggested'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: The tutor suggested to taking short breaks every 45 minutes to improve concentration.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Adding '-ing' to 'taking' is a step in the right direction, but keeping 'to' before it creates 'to taking', which isn't grammatically possible — just use 'taking' on its own.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: The tutor suggested that take short breaks every 45 minutes to improve concentration.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Suggested that take' skips the subject needed after 'that' — if you use the 'that' clause route, it must be 'suggested that he/she take', which adds complexity; the simplest fix is 'suggested taking'.

commonWrongAnswers.answer: The tutor suggested to have short breaks every 45 minutes to improve concentration.
commonWrongAnswers.comment: Swapping 'take' for 'have' changes the phrasing but keeps the same error — 'to have' is still a to-infinitive, and 'suggest' never takes that form.

questions.context: A student is writing an email to her professor: 'My previous tutor told me that if I practised writing every day, my essay scores ________ (improve) significantly within a month.'
questions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct modal past form to complete the reported conditional sentence.
questions.hint: The tutor's original words were probably 'your scores will improve' — what happens to 'will' in reported speech?
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' shifts back to 'would', so 'will improve' from the original statement becomes 'would improve' in the reported version.

commonWrongAnswers.comment: 'Will' is the tutor's original word, but once you move it into reported speech after a past verb like 'told', 'will' must shift to 'would'.
'Could' suggests possibility or ability rather than a confident prediction — the tutor was saying the scores would definitely get better, not just that they might.
'Would have improved' suggests the condition was not met (a third conditional idea), but the student is simply reporting what the tutor predicted, not expressing regret about the past.
